name: Jimaku
description: Finds Japanese subtitles for anime episodes on jimaku.cc, verifies the candidate against the local file's actual timing (embedded subtitle track, or voice activity in the Japanese audio), corrects constant offsets and framerate drift, and writes the result as an external .jpn.ass / .jpn.srt sidecar. Declines rather than guessing when confidence is low. (Requires a Jimaku API key.)
overview: Japanese subtitles from Jimaku, timing-verified against your media

versions.changelog:
- Expose the two limits governing differing-cut matching: how many sections a subtitle may be
  split into, and how few lines a section may contain. Both were only reachable by editing the
  configuration file.

- Actually try the differing-cut aligner on differently-cut subtitles. The attempt was gated on
  the global correlation being halfway decent, which is backwards: a subtitle cut differently has
  no single offset that works, so its global correlation is low by construction. The guard now
  sits on the split's own result, where it already was.
- Say what the piecewise attempt found when it fell short, rather than reporting a bare decline.
  A split that reached 0.48 against a floor of 0.50 says the file is probably right.
- Offer the measured correction when applying a file by hand. "Use anyway" wrote it unchanged,
  which is the worst outcome when the file is simply misaligned - now you can take the measured
  shift on your own judgement, or type an exact one.

- Use image-based subtitle tracks as a timing reference. A PGS or VobSub track carries no text,
  but every display set has a presentation timestamp, so its timings are stated outright in the
  packet headers - and timings are the only thing alignment ever uses. Disc rips, which most
  often carry nothing but picture subtitles, are also where the audio fallback is weakest.
- Read those timings with ffprobe alone: packet headers, no decoding and nothing written to disk.
  Erase segments are folded into the cue they end rather than counted as cues of their own, which
  would otherwise have doubled the cue count and halved every gap.

- Read embedded subtitle tracks straight from the item instead of through a media source. When
  resolving that source failed, the whole search gave up before listing anything, so a file full
  of subtitle tracks reported having none - and said so only at debug level.
- Fall back to extracting by stream index when extraction by path fails, so one broken route no
  longer costs the reference entirely.
- Use Jellyfin's own definition of a text subtitle track rather than a list of codec names, which
  could be defeated by a spelling this plugin had not seen.
- Log the reason each track could not be read at warning level, and show it per track. Every one
  of these failing is the most likely reason a file with good subtitles falls back to audio, and
  it was invisible.
- Name image-based tracks as the cause when they are. A PGS track appears in Jellyfin's subtitle
  menu like any other, so a file can look well supplied while carrying nothing readable.

- Say what the timing was compared against. A new per-episode view lists every embedded subtitle
  track, whether it could be read, how many cues it had and which one was used - so an episode
  whose tracks are all image-based is no longer indistinguishable from one where a signs track
  was picked.
- Explain a decline caused by the reference rather than the subtitles. When the comparison fell
  back to voice activity, the message now says why, and that energy-based detection is weak for
  anime.
- Stop reporting "covers 0% of dialogue" when coverage could not be measured at all. A voice
  activity reference has no cue structure to compare against, and zero read as a verdict on the
  subtitle.
- Sort signs and songs tracks below dialogue when choosing a reference, and say so when one is
  all that is available.

- Bring episodes synced by earlier versions into the new tracking. Those records held only the
  last outcome, so the sidecar was never cleaned up when replaced, deleting it taught nothing and
  the reject action reported that nothing was attached.
- Discard release-group preferences learned before automatic picks stopped counting. A preference
  a sweep confirmed for itself is circular rather than weak, and there is no record of which
  confirmations were yours, so it is dropped and rebuilds from your own picks. Cached Jimaku
  searches are kept.
- Show a series' preferred group on its episode list, with how much stands behind it and a button
  to forget it.
- Add "replace subtitles that are already there" to the series and season sweeps, so a season can
  be redone once you have picked the right group by hand.

- Only count subtitles you picked yourself towards a series' preferred release group. A bulk run
  confirming the preference that produced it was the plugin marking its own work, and it
  compounds: whatever the first sweep landed on would bias the next episode and confirm itself
  again. Rejections still count however the file got there.
- Sweep a chosen series or season from the plugin page, rather than only whole libraries nightly.
- Show what a sweep is actually doing. The Scheduled Tasks page renders only a name and a
  percentage, so the running episode and tally now appear in the task's name there, and in full
  on the plugin page - which episode, what was attached, and why anything was declined - for a
  run started from either place. It can be stopped from there too.

- Keep a record of what was attached to each episode. The sidecar's filename is derived from the
  media file, so nothing on disk said which Jimaku upload it came from; the plugin now tracks
  every attempt, and writes the source file name into the subtitle itself.
- Treat deleting a subtitle as rejecting it. That file is no longer chosen automatically for the
  episode, and the credit it gave the series' preferred release group is taken back. Picking it
  explicitly still works.
- Remove the subtitle being replaced instead of leaving it behind under a ".1." counter, so an
  episode stops accumulating sidecars the player can choose between. Only ever a file the plugin
  recorded writing, or one carrying its own stamp.
- Add a "what's attached?" view per episode, with a button to reject the current subtitle.

- Tell the client when a subtitle is actually attached. Jellyfin's own dialog says "download
  queued" and then nothing; the plugin now sends its own message once the work is finished, and
  records the outcome in Dashboard - Activity.
- Remember which release group works for a series. Once several episodes have been served
  correctly by the same group, later episodes prefer it - but only to break a close call, never
  over a measurably better match.
- Reuse a series' Jimaku search across its episodes. Searching once per episode spent half a
  sweep's request budget re-asking a settled question.
- Cap the scheduled sweep and run it newest-first, with an option to only look at recently added
  episodes. The rate limit was always respected; a first run could still saturate it for hours.
- Pick libraries to sweep with checkboxes. The multi-select gave no visible indication of what
  was actually selected.

- Choose the timing reference by agreement between the embedded tracks, not by cue count. The
  densest track is often the group's own, carrying karaoke and signs and timed differently.
- Rank candidates on how much dialogue they actually cover, not only on how well they align.
  A subtitle that omits lines and holds them briefly no longer beats a fuller one.
- Stop demoting subtitles whose filename does not state a language; only bilingual releases
  are ranked down now.
- Identify a subtitle's language by reading it rather than by parsing its filename, so an
  untagged Japanese file is recognised and a bilingual one is caught however it is named.
- Fix the choice between the two ways of comparing timings, which preferred the one that then
  failed its own threshold and caused every candidate to be declined.
- Cache the timing reference per episode, so listing candidates and then applying one no longer
  repeats the most expensive step.
- Add Jimaku to the main menu.
